did_you_know.text: Did you know? 1 Chronicles 20 describes Joab going out to war “at the time when kings go out to battle,” meaning the season suitable for kings to campaign. Joab devastated the land of the Ammonites, besieged Rabbah, and eventually captured it, while David remained in Jerusalem.

Did you know? After capturing Rabbah, David took the crown of their king from his head. The crown weighed a talent of gold and was set with a precious stone. David also carried away a great deal of plunder from the city.

Did you know? The text says that David brought out the people of Rabbah and put them to hard labor with saws, iron picks, and axes. According to the verse, he did the same in all the cities of the Ammonites, after which David and the people returned to Jerusalem.

Did you know? In the battle at Gezer, Sibbecai the Hushathite struck down Sippai, who was descended from the Rephaim, and the Philistines were subdued. The chapter goes on to describe several victories by Israel’s warriors over exceptionally large fighters.

Did you know? In another battle with the Philistines, Elhanan son of Jair struck down Lahmi, the brother of Goliath the Gittite. The text emphasizes that Lahmi’s spear shaft was like a weaver’s beam—that is, large and thick like the beam used on a loom.

Did you know? One of the Philistine warriors is described as having six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot—a total of twenty-four digits. He too was descended from the Rephaim and fought at Gath.
Did you know? When the man with twenty-four digits taunted Israel, Jonathan son of Shimeah, David’s brother, struck him down. In this way, the chapter presents Jonathan as one of Israel’s warriors.
Did you know? At the end of the account, it says that all four of these large warriors were descendants of the Rephaim in Gath, and all of them fell at the hands of David and his servants.
